content: 1. The Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease receives an honorarium for his role. 2. Dalene von Delft disclosed receiving financial and logistical support from organizations such as TAG, USAID, UNITAID, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Critical Path to TB Drug Regimens (CPTR), and AERAS to cover travel and accommodation costs for presentations and speeches on drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB). 3. In 2011, Dalene von Delft received bedaquiline as part of her treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) through a compassionate use access program. 4. Gregory J. Fox declared receiving research and non-monetary support from The Union, sponsored by Otsuka, valued at approximately USD 5,000, to attend the 2015 International Union Conference and to receive the Young Innovator Award. He clarified that he has no professional relationship with Otsuka or any commercial or research activities related to the award. 5. Katherine Fielding disclosed that her employer, the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), received an award from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) amounting to £26,890 for statistical support for the TB-PRACTECAL study, a Phase II–III randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating the efficacy and safety of shorter MDR-TB regimens for adults. She is a co-investigator in this study. 6. Rebecca Harris declared consulting for a clinical research organization, Cromsource, working for GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) vaccines, earning approximately £90,000 in 2013. She also worked on GSK vaccines unrelated to TB, earning approximately £10,000 since 2013 for Manpower Solutions. 7. David Moore disclosed receiving research support from the Wellcome Trust Research Training Fellowship Programme to supervise a PhD student studying MDR-TB in Peru, with funding amounting to £207,056 in 2014. 8. Anneke Hesseling declared that her employer, Stellenbosch University, received an award from Otsuka Pharmaceutical, amounting to approximately USD 7,000 to date, for her work on Phase III delamanid clinical trials in children. 9. Funding for the meetings and reviews involved in updating the 2011 WHO guidelines for the programmatic management of drug-resistant tuberculosis came entirely from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). 10. Experts on the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and their institutions contributed time to discussions and activities related to the guideline update process. 11. Declaration of interest forms were completed by all non-WHO members of the GDG, the External Review Group, and members of academic centers involved in the reviews. 12. Four GDG members declared interests judged to represent potential conflicts and were excused from sessions during the October 25–27, 2010, meeting where recommendations on drug regimens were discussed. 13. Jaime Bayona served as a consultant for the development of clinical trial designs for studies of an anti-tuberculosis drug manufactured by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd (OPC-67683). 14. Charles L. Daley chaired drug-safety monitoring for two trials conducted by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd. 15. Carole D. Mitnick was a member of the Scientific Advisory Board of Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd and had an advisory role on drug OPC-67683. 16. Ma. Imelda Quelapio received monetary and non-monetary support for research from Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd. 17. Members of academic centers who reviewed evidence for the recommendations in the guidelines presented their findings at the meeting. These members included Matthew Arentz, Melissa Bauer, Richard Menzies, Carole D. Mitnick, Olivia Oxlade, Patricia Pavlinac, and Judd L. Watson. They did not participate in formulating recommendations related to their respective evidence reviews. 18. The WHO treatment guidelines for multidrugand rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) were updated in 2020. 19. The question addressed in the guidelines was whether an all-oral shorter regimen of 9–12 months, including bedaquiline, should be used for MDR/RR-TB patients to safely improve outcomes compared to a shorter regimen recommended by WHO that includes injectables. 20. The certainty of evidence for the outcomes assessed in the guidelines was rated as very low, with critical importance assigned to the findings. 21. The guidelines also evaluated whether an all-oral shorter regimen of 9–12 months, including bedaquiline, should be used compared to longer regimens without new TB drugs. 22. The evidence for the outcomes in this comparison was also rated as very low certainty, with critical importance. 23. Another question addressed was whether an all-oral shorter regimen of 9–12 months, including bedaquiline, should be used compared to longer regimens containing bedaquiline. 24. The certainty of evidence for this comparison was similarly rated as very low, with critical importance. 25. The guidelines included detailed GRADE evidence summary tables assessing the certainty of evidence, the number of patients, and the effects of different regimens on outcomes such as treatment success and loss to follow-up. 26. The guidelines emphasized the importance of considering the very low certainty of evidence when interpreting the findings and making clinical decisions.
